reuse.text: Welcome, explorers. Our journey has brought us to Mars. Look below. That research base once helped people learn how to live here.
Oh! You are new. I am NEILO. You are the first visitor in a very long time. Shall we explore together?
We are safe in orbit. It is wonderful to hear from the base. Prepare your supplies, then send us your ready signal. We will plan the next step together.
There it goes. Your first signal! You gave every system its turn. And now your crew knows we are here. Together.
Every active device shares the same power supply. You can switch optional devices off and run important jobs one at a time.
Before you run a device, check its supplies and the power it needs. Look at the whole base, then choose what to run first.
Start with a check, then prepare the antenna. When the base is ready, test your message before you send it.
Keep essential life-support systems running while you work. Take time to prepare the base before starting a new task.
Tap the floor to walk. See that little blue light? Tap it to take a closer look.
I’ll walk with you. Tap the floor to explore, or choose a glowing object. Tap me whenever you need a hand.
A guidance fault. Fasten your harness. Your safety capsule will take you down to the research base. We are safe in orbit.
Your capsule is approaching the base. Once inside, follow the lights.
The base is quiet. Beneath the workbench, a small robot waits. Take a closer look.

new_lines.text: Plants need suitable light, water, nutrients, temperature and air. Our two switches represent only part of that environment.
CSA lists about 21–28 days for leaf lettuce and 45–65 days for soybeans. Our planner used the upper end of each range. Real growing conditions can change the result.
The example soybeans need boiling. Lettuce can be eaten without cooking. Crops add different nutrients to meals, alongside stored food.
A new crop needs cooking. What should the crew include in its plan?
RAD aboard Curiosity measured radiation on Mars. Our archive shows 84 absorbed dose rate readings, in micrograys per hour, from 1 January 2015.
In a separate 2016 study at Butte M12, surrounding terrain blocked part of the sky. Researchers found a 4% decrease in expected dose rate there.
A missing value means that measurement is unavailable. A reading at one place does not tell us whether another site is safe.
The new site has no radiation reading. What belongs in your report?

source.title: NASA Space Place · What powers a spacecraft?

new_lines.text: Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity. Some spacecraft use sunlight to run their equipment.

source.title: NASA Space Place · What powers a spacecraft?

new_lines.text: A battery stores energy. Spacecraft can use that stored energy when sunlight is unavailable.

source.title: NASA Space Place · What powers a spacecraft?

new_lines.text: An electric motor transfers energy into motion. In our base, the pump uses part of the battery reserve.
When the solar panels are in shadow, what can provide stored energy?
On Hubble, electricity powers instruments, computers, heaters and transmitters.
Running more devices at once asks for more power. In our base, the pump and radio together exceed the supply limit.
Pausing one job made room for the next. The battery reserve showed how much stored energy remained.
If two jobs exceed the supply limit, what could you try?
Listen. There is a little blue light under that bench. Shall we look?
The pump and the radio share our power. Which job shall we try first?
Let’s test your plan. Watch the connections and the devices.
That branch needs more power than we have left. What could we pause?
You chose water first. The tank is ready, and our message can have the next turn.
You reached the crew first. Now let’s get our water ready for the wait.
Good change. Your new plan gives that device enough power.
I found seed packets. Let’s plan a fresh addition to the crew’s meals.
Look at the harvest window and the kitchen tool. Which crop fits your plan?
Seeds need a suitable environment. Check the light and water connections.
This is our training calendar. We can watch weeks pass in the simulation.
The planned meal date is here, but this crop needs more time. Stored meals can cover the wait.
Your tray is ready. Let’s harvest it and check how to prepare it.
These soybeans need boiling before we serve them.
A new request from the crew. We have more time, and they want a crop that contains protein.
You changed your plan when the meal request changed. That is what a good planner does.
The crew needs our field notes. The robot has a relay to repair and evidence to gather. Which comes first?
This is Curiosity’s archive from January twenty fifteen. Read the device, the date, and the unit.
A dash means this measurement is not available. It does not mean zero.
The cliff study is from a different time and place. Let’s keep its evidence separate.
That new site still needs a measurement. We can say what we know and what we need to check.
The report is sent. Our relay is still waiting for its turn.
Take another look at the part that is glowing. What changed when you tried your plan?
I can show you one step. Then you can try the next one.
Your choices brought this base to life. I have saved our plans in the journey log.
